$$x\cdot y=\sum_{j=1}^3x_jy_j\quad(x,y\in\mathbb R^3),\qquad a\cdot b=\sum_{j=1}^3a_jb_j\quad(a,b\in\mathbb C^3),$$
where the second dot product is the complex-bilinear extension. The fiber
Hermitian pairing is $\overline a\cdot b=\sum_j\overline{a_j}b_j$, with
norm $|a|^2=\sum_j|a_j|^2$. Set
$$\mathcal H=L^2(\mathbb R^3,d^3\mathbf k;\mathbb C^3),\qquad \langle u,v\rangle_2=\int_{\mathbb R^3}\overline{u(\mathbf k)}\cdot v(\mathbf k)\,d^3\mathbf k,$$
Here $d^3\mathbf k$ is Lebesgue measure, and this pairing is
second-variable-linear. For $\mathbf k\ne0$,
put $\widehat{\mathbf k}=\mathbf k/|\mathbf k|$
and $P_T(\mathbf k)=I_3-\widehat{\mathbf k}\widehat{\mathbf k}^{T}$, the
Euclidean orthogonal projection onto the fiber plane perpendicular to
$\mathbf k$; assign any value at $\mathbf k=0$. Its multiplier is an
orthogonal projection on $\mathcal H$, so its range is closed. The transverse
one-particle Hilbert space
is
$$\mathcal H_T=\operatorname{Ran}M_{P_T}=\{u\in\mathcal H:\mathbf k\cdot u(\mathbf k)=0\text{ for a.e. }\mathbf k\ne0\},$$
where $M_{P_T}$ is multiplication by $P_T$, and the real Euclidean dot
product is extended complex-bilinearly in the transverse condition. This is
the transverse one-particle space used in this model.

For $m\ge1$, use the iterated Hilbert tensor completion
$\mathcal H_T^{\widehat\otimes m}$, with product pairing on elementary
tensors. Here $S_m$ is the permutation group and
$U_\pi(u_1\otimes\cdots\otimes u_m)=
u_{\pi^{-1}(1)}\otimes\cdots\otimes u_{\pi^{-1}(m)}$. Set
$$P_{s,m}=\frac1{m!}\sum_{\pi\in S_m}U_\pi,\qquad \mathcal H_s^{(m)}=\operatorname{Ran}P_{s,m};$$
put $P_{s,0}=I_{\mathbb C}$ and $\mathcal H_s^{(0)}=\mathbb C$. The
symmetric bosonic Fock space is
$$\mathcal F_s(\mathcal H_T)=\left\{(\Psi_m)_{m\ge0}:\Psi_m\in\mathcal H_s^{(m)},\ \sum_{m\ge0}\|\Psi_m\|^2<\infty\right\},$$
with componentwise pairing and vacuum $1\in\mathbb C$ in sector zero.
For $f\in\mathcal H_T$, define the exponential-vector map
$\epsilon:\mathcal H_T\to\mathcal F_s(\mathcal H_T)$ by
$$\epsilon(f)=\bigoplus_{m=0}^{\infty}\frac{P_{s,m}(f^{\otimes m})}{\sqrt{m!}}.$$
Here $f^{\otimes0}=1$ in the vacuum sector.
Since $f^{\otimes m}$ is already symmetric,
$P_{s,m}(f^{\otimes m})=f^{\otimes m}$ for $m\ge1$; write this tensor as
$f^{\otimes_s m}$.

For fixed angular-frequency cutoffs $0<\varepsilon<\Delta<\Lambda$, let
$\nu(\mathbf k)=c|\mathbf k|$ in s$^{-1}$, with $\mathbf k$ in m$^{-1}$.
The one-particle coherent displacement is the transverse mode function
$$f_{\varepsilon,\Lambda}(\mathbf k)= \mathbf1_{\{\varepsilon<\nu(\mathbf k)<\Lambda\}}|\mathbf k|^{-3/2} {}\times b\!\left(\frac{\mathbf k}{|\mathbf k|}\right) \quad(\mathbf k\ne0), \qquad f_{\varepsilon,\Lambda}(0)=0.$$
The function $f_{\varepsilon,\Lambda}$ has units m$^{3/2}$ in
$\mathcal H_T$; the associated free one-photon energy is
$\hbar\nu(\mathbf k)=\hbar c|\mathbf k|$ in J. Define its normalized
coherent vector by
$$\Psi_{\varepsilon,\Lambda}=\exp\!\left(-\frac{\|f_{\varepsilon,\Lambda}\|^2}{2}\right)\epsilon(f_{\varepsilon,\Lambda}).$$
For a finite partition
$B_1,\ldots,B_r$ of $(\varepsilon,\Lambda)$ into disjoint Borel intervals,
let
$H_j=\{u\in\mathcal H_T:u(\mathbf k)=0\text{ a.e. unless }\nu(\mathbf k)\in B_j\}$.
Let $P_j$ be multiplication on $\mathcal H_T$ by
$\mathbf1_{\{\nu(\mathbf k)\in B_j\}}$. This bounded self-adjoint idempotent
preserves transversality because it is scalar-valued, so it is an orthogonal
projection. Its range is exactly $H_j$, making $H_j$ closed. For $j\ne k$,
disjointness gives $P_jP_k=0$, hence the ranges are orthogonal.
For a tuple $(m_1,\ldots,m_r)\in\mathbb N_0^r$, put $M=\sum_jm_j$.
Its occupation subspace is the closed span in sector $\mathcal H_s^{(M)}$
of the vectors
$$P_{s,M}\left(\bigotimes_{j=1}^r\bigotimes_{\ell=1}^{m_j}u_{j,\ell}\right),\qquad u_{j,\ell}\in H_j,$$
where the empty tensor for $M=0$ is the vacuum $1\in\mathbb C$. It has
exactly $m_j$ factors in $H_j$ and no factor outside $\bigoplus_jH_j$.
Define $N(B_j)$ to have value $m_j$ on this subspace.
The model assigns the tuple
probability equal to the squared norm of the projection of
$\Psi_{\varepsilon,\Lambda}$ onto it. Its resolution parameter
$\Delta$ divides $(\varepsilon,\Lambda)$ into the unresolved band
$(\varepsilon,\Delta)$ and the resolved band $[\Delta,\Lambda)$. The
threshold frequency is assigned to the resolved band; its exact assignment
does not change any $L^2$ vector or probability because a single frequency
has zero one-particle measure.
This is a finite-cutoff free coherent-state model; it does not posit a
detector response or an interacting QED scattering law.

Fix the finite-leg current data and cutoffs of the resolved-soft model. For every
finite partition $B_1,\ldots,B_r$ of $(\varepsilon,\Lambda)$ into disjoint
Borel frequency intervals, the coherent state
$\Psi_{\varepsilon,\Lambda}$ has independent band counts. For each $j$,
$N(B_j)$ has Poisson distribution with mean
$$\lambda_j=C\int_{B_j}\frac{d\nu}{\nu},$$
where $\nu$ is angular frequency in s$^{-1}$. Thus
$\lambda_j=C\log(b_j/a_j)$ for an interval with endpoints
$0<a_j<b_j$; endpoint conventions do not matter because $d\nu/\nu$
assigns a singleton zero measure. For $C=0$ every band count is zero.
The model's marked frequency density is the one-particle coherent
intensity $|b(n)|^2\,d\Omega(n)\,d\nu/\nu$.

For an integer $d\ge1$, let $\mathcal S(\mathbb R^d)$ be the complex Schwartz space with seminorms
$p_{\alpha\beta}(f)=\sup_{x\in\mathbb R^d}|x^\alpha\partial^\beta f(x)|$
for all multi-indices $\alpha,\beta$; this is exactly
[[def-schwartz-space-and-its-seminorms]]. Let
$\mathcal D(\mathbb R^d)=C_c^\infty(\mathbb R^d;\mathbb C)$ with the support convention of
[[def-test-function-space-d-of-an-open-set]] and the locally convex LF topology of
[[def-test-function-topology]]. The tempered-distribution space $\mathcal S'(\mathbb R^d)$
is the space of continuous complex-linear functionals on this topological
$\mathcal S(\mathbb R^d)$, paired bilinearly with test functions, as in
[[def-tempered-distribution]].

For every complex Hilbert space $H$, use the second-variable-linear pairing
$\langle u,v\rangle_2:=(v,u)_1$, where $(\cdot,\cdot)_1$ is the first-variable-linear
Hilbert pairing of [[def-real-and-complex-inner-product-space]]. Thus
$\langle u,v\rangle_2$ is linear in $v$ and conjugate-linear in $u$.
For each tensor product, use the same norm completion as
[[lem-nrqm-composites-hilbert-tensor-construction]], but equip it with the
second-variable-linear pairing obtained by conjugating that supplier's
first-variable-linear pairing. This leaves the norm and completion unchanged;
on elementary tensors it gives the product of the second-variable pairings.
Let $H^{\widehat\otimes n}$ be the iterated Hilbert tensor completion, with
$H^{\widehat\otimes0}:=\mathbb C$; the tensor inner product is the product of
the factor pairings. Identify parenthesizations by the isometry fixing
elementary tensors: the product pairing is the same on their dense span,
so the map and its inverse extend to the completions. For $n\ge1$, let
$P_{s,n}=n!^{-1}\sum_{\pi\in S_n}U_\pi$ and
$P_{a,n}=n!^{-1}\sum_{\pi\in S_n}\operatorname{sgn}(\pi)U_\pi$, using the
permutation action and the orthogonal projections of
[[lem-nrqm-composites-permutation-sector-projections]]. Define
$H_s^{(n)}=\operatorname{ran}P_{s,n}$ and
$H_a^{(n)}=\operatorname{ran}P_{a,n}$, with
$H_s^{(0)}=H_a^{(0)}=\mathbb C$. These are the symmetric and antisymmetric
$n$-particle sectors.

The bosonic and fermionic Fock Hilbert spaces are the square-summable direct
sums
$\mathcal F_s(H)=\{(\Psi_n)_{n\ge0}:\Psi_n\in H_s^{(n)},\
\sum_n\|\Psi_n\|^2<\infty\}$ and
$\mathcal F_a(H)=\{(\Psi_n)_{n\ge0}:\Psi_n\in H_a^{(n)},\
\sum_n\|\Psi_n\|^2<\infty\}$, with the componentwise inner product.
Their vacuum is $\Omega=(1,0,0,\ldots)$. The finite-particle subspace
$\mathcal D_{\rm fin}$ consists of sequences with only finitely many nonzero
components.

For $h\in H$, the map $C_h:H\to\mathbb C$, $C_h(v)=\langle h,v\rangle_2$, is linear and bounded:
$|C_h(v)|=|(v,h)_1|\le\|h\|\,\|v\|$ by
[[thm-cauchy-schwarz-for-real-and-complex-inner-product-spaces]].
For any Hilbert space $K$, identify $\mathbb C\widehat\otimes K$ with $K$
by $J_K(z\otimes v)=zv$. Every algebraic tensor is $1\otimes w$;
the tensor norm is then $\|w\|$, so $J_K$ extends to a surjective isometry
on the completion (with inverse $w\mapsto1\otimes w$).
Throughout the following formulas, $C_h\otimes I^{\otimes(n-1)}$ means
$J_{H^{\widehat\otimes(n-1)}}\circ(C_h\widehat\otimes I)$, with
$I$ the identity on $H^{\widehat\otimes(n-1)}$.
The bounded tensor-map supplier therefore applies and gives norm at most
$\|h\|$. This includes $n=1$, where $H^{\widehat\otimes0}=\mathbb C$.
Contraction commutes with permutations of the remaining $n-1$ factors,
so it takes symmetric or antisymmetric tensors to the corresponding
$(n-1)$-particle sector (and to $\mathbb C$ for $n=1$).

For $n\ge0$, bosonic creation on sector $n$ is
$a_n^\dagger(h)\Psi_n=\sqrt{n+1}P_{s,n+1}(h\otimes\Psi_n)$; for $n\ge1$,
bosonic annihilation is
$a_n(h)\Psi_n=\sqrt n(C_h\otimes I^{\otimes(n-1)})\Psi_n$, where
$C_h$ is the bounded functional above, its tensor extension is supplied by
[[lem-nrqm-composites-bounded-tensor-maps]], and $a(h)\Omega=0$. Define fermionic creation
by $c_n^\dagger(h)\Psi_n=\sqrt{n+1}P_{a,n+1}(h\otimes\Psi_n)$; for $n\ge1$,
fermionic annihilation is the corresponding first-factor contraction
$c_n(h)\Psi_n=\sqrt n(C_h\otimes I^{\otimes(n-1)})\Psi_n$, and
$c(h)\Omega=0$. The annihilation maps are conjugate-linear in $h$; the
creation maps are linear in $h$. These formulas define sector maps on the
finite-particle subspace; their maximal closed domains and operator relations are proved in
[[lem-qft-fock-ccr-car]]. No physical statistics assignment or spin–statistics
theorem is part of these mathematical definitions.

Assume Countable Choice [[def-countable-choice]]. Let
$$\mathcal H=L^2(\mathbb R^3,d^3\mathbf k;\mathbb C^3),\qquad \langle u,v\rangle_2=\int_{\mathbb R^3}\overline{u(\mathbf k)}\cdot v(\mathbf k)\,d^3\mathbf k,$$
with the second-variable-linear convention of [[def-qft-fock-and-test-spaces]]; the real momentum dot product and norm are those of
[[def-euclidean-inner-product]]. Explicitly extend the real dot product
complex-bilinearly to $a\cdot b=\sum_{j=1}^3a_jb_j$ for $a,b\in\mathbb C^3$.
Each complex fiber instead has the positive Hermitian pairing
$\langle a,b\rangle_2=\overline a\cdot b=\sum_j\overline a_jb_j$ and
norm $\|a\|^2=\sum_j|a_j|^2$; the displayed integral uses this pairing.
Hilbert completeness follows from [[lem-l-two-with-the-integral-pairing-is-a-hilbert-space]]. For $\mathbf k\ne0$, write $n(\mathbf k)=\mathbf k/|\mathbf k|$ and
$$P_T(\mathbf k)=I_3-n(\mathbf k)n(\mathbf k)^T.$$
Assign any value at $\mathbf k=0$, which is a Lebesgue-null set. Let $M_{P_T}$ be multiplication by this measurable matrix field and define the positive transverse photon space
$$\mathcal H_T=\operatorname{Ran}M_{P_T} =\{u\in\mathcal H:\mathbf k\cdot u(\mathbf k)=0\text{ for almost every }\mathbf k\ne0\}.$$
The inner product on $\mathcal H_T$ is the restriction of that on $\mathcal H$. Each nonzero momentum fiber is the two-complex-dimensional plane $\{a\in\mathbb C^3:\mathbf k\cdot a=0\}$ perpendicular to the real vector $\mathbf k$ in that Hermitian pairing; no global continuous polarization frame is part of the definition.

Assume Countable Choice [[def-countable-choice]]. Use the transverse space $\mathcal H_T=\operatorname{Ran}M_{P_T}$ of [[def-qft-photon-transverse-space]], with $P_T(\mathbf k)=I_3-\mathbf n\mathbf n^T$ for $\mathbf k\ne0$ and any assigned value at the null point $\mathbf k=0$. In the QFT length convention, assign $\mathbf k$ units m$^{-1}$ and define the nonnegative measurable multiplier
$$ \omega(\mathbf k):=|\mathbf k|. $$
Its maximal multiplication operator on $\mathcal H_T$ is
$$ (M_\omega f)(\mathbf k):=\omega(\mathbf k)f(\mathbf k),\qquad D(M_\omega):=\{f\in\mathcal H_T:\omega f\in L^2(\mathbb R^3,d^3\mathbf k;\mathbb C^3)\}. $$
Because $\omega$ is a scalar multiplier, $\mathbf k\cdot f(\mathbf k)=0$ a.e. implies $\mathbf k\cdot(M_\omega f)(\mathbf k)=0$ a.e.; thus the displayed multiplication maps its stated domain into $\mathcal H_T$. The value $\omega(0)=0$ is immaterial to the $L^2$ operator. For $\hbar,c>0$, the corresponding one-particle energy convention is $E_1:=\hbar c M_\omega$, in joules.

Assume Countable Choice [[def-countable-choice]]. Let
$(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be a sigma-finite measure space and let
$\boldsymbol\omega=(\omega_1,\ldots,\omega_d):X\to\mathbb R^d$ be a
finite-valued measurable map, where $d\ge1$. Put
$H=L^2(X,\mu;\mathbb C)$ with the second-variable-linear pairing of
[[def-qft-fock-and-test-spaces]], and form the bosonic Fock space
$\mathcal F_s(H)$. For $n\ge1$, identify $H_s^{(n)}$ with the symmetric
subspace of $L^2(X^n,\overline{\mu^{\times n}};\mathbb C)$ by iterating
[[lem-qft-l2-product-tensor-identification]]. Set $X^0=\{\star\}$,
$s_0(\star)=0$, and for $n\ge1$ set
$$s_n(x_1,\ldots,x_n)=\sum_{r=1}^n\boldsymbol\omega(x_r)\in\mathbb R^d.$$
For $1\le j\le d$, define $H_j$ by multiplication by the $j$th coordinate
$s_{n,j}$ on sector $n$, with exact domain
$$D(H_j)=\left\{\Psi=(\Psi_n): \sum_{n\ge1}\int_{X^n}|s_{n,j}|^2|\Psi_n|^2\,d\overline{\mu^{\times n}}<\infty\right\}.$$
Each $H_j$ is self-adjoint, and $\mathcal D_{\rm fin}\cap D(H_j)$ is a
graph core. The joint projection-valued measure
[[def-projection-valued-measure]] on $\mathbb R^d$ is
$$(E(B)\Psi)_n=\mathbf1_{s_n^{-1}(B)}\Psi_n\quad(n\ge1),\qquad (E(B)\Psi)_0=\mathbf1_B(0)\Psi_0.$$
For $\theta\in\mathbb R^d$, let $H_\theta$ be multiplication on sector $n$
by $\theta\cdot s_n$, with its maximal square-integrability domain. Then
$$U_\theta(t)\Psi:=\bigl(e^{it\theta\cdot s_n}\Psi_n\bigr)_{n\ge0}$$
is a strongly continuous unitary group on all of Fock space, and its norm
derivative at zero exists exactly for $\Psi\in D(H_\theta)$, where it is
$iH_\theta\Psi$. The zero-particle sector is the vacuum eigenvector at joint
value $0$.

Assume the $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ convention of [[def-bounded-c-one-domain-boundary-charts-and-outward-normal]]. Let S be a compact embedded $C^1$ hypersurface in $\mathbb R^n$, $n\ge2$. Choose finitely many regular injective $C^1$ parametrizations $X_j:V_j\to S\cap O_j$ with $C^1$ coordinate transitions, and an ambient partition $\chi_j$ from [[lem-finite-ambient-partitions-for-euclidean-boundary-integration]], with supports compactly contained in the corresponding chart neighborhoods. Put $J_{X_j}=\sqrt{\det(DX_j^TDX_j)}$, using [[def-gram-matrix-and-gram-determinant]].

For a nonnegative Borel f on S define $\int_S f\,dS=\sum_j\int_{V_j}(\chi_j f)(X_j(y))J_{X_j}(y)\,dy$, where the integrals on the right are those of [[def-nonnegative-lebesgue-integral]] and $0\cdot\infty=0$. Set $S(A)=\int_S\mathbf1_A\,dS$ for Borel A. For signed f with $\int_S|f|\,dS<\infty$ use the difference of the positive and negative integrals. The same chart formula restricts to a compact Borel face contained in a regular patch. The empty surface has zero integral. Independence and finiteness are established by the following chart-independence lemma.

Assume $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ and $n\ge2$. The chart surface measure on $S^{n-1}$ equals the polar measure $\sigma$. Orthogonal transformations preserve it. The map $\omega\mapsto a+R\omega$, $R>0$, multiplies surface measure by $R^{n-1}$, and $|S^{n-1}|=n|B_1|$.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let $n \ge 1$,
let $S^{n-1} \subseteq \mathbb R^n$ be the unit sphere, and let $\sigma$ be the
set function of [[def-polar-surface-measure-on-the-unit-sphere]]. Then $\sigma$
is a finite Borel measure on $S^{n-1}$, and for every Borel measurable
$f : \mathbb R^n \to [0,\infty]$,
$$\int_{\mathbb R^n} f(x)\,d\lambda_n(x) = \int_0^\infty \int_{S^{n-1}} f(r\omega) r^{n-1}\,d\sigma(\omega)\,dr.$$
Moreover, $\sigma$ is the unique Borel measure on $S^{n-1}$ with this
property.

For $x>0$, $\log$ is differentiable and
$$\log'(x)=\frac1x,\qquad \log x=\int_1^x\frac{dt}{t}.$$

Let $\iota_{\mathbb R}\colon\mathbb N\to\mathbb R$ be the canonical-natural map
of [[def-canonical-natural]], and let $j\colon\mathbb R\to\mathbb C$ be the real
embedding $j(x)=x+i0$ from [[def-complex-numbers-and-arithmetic]]. For every
$n\in\mathbb N$, the factorial $n!$ is nonzero by
[[def-factorial-and-falling-factorial]], so
$\iota_{\mathbb R}(n!)>0$ by [[lem-of-naturals-positive]] and consequently
$j(\iota_{\mathbb R}(n!))\ne0$ in the complex field
[[thm-complex-numbers-form-a-field]].

For $z\in\mathbb C$, define
$$ \exp z:=\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}\frac{z^n}{j(\iota_{\mathbb R}(n!))}. $$
whenever this complex series converges. Inside a complex expression we
abbreviate the embedded denominator $j(\iota_{\mathbb R}(n!))$ by $n!$, so the
same definition may be written $\exp z=\sum z^n/n!$ without identifying a
natural number with a complex number. Powers and series are those of
[[def-complex-integer-powers]] and
[[def-complex-series-power-series-and-absolute-convergence]]. The convergence
for every $z\in\mathbb C$ is discharged by
[[lem-complex-exponential-series-converges-everywhere]].
For every $z\in\mathbb C$, the series $\sum z^n/n!$ converges absolutely.

For all $z,w\in\mathbb C$, $\exp(z+w)=\exp z\exp w$. For real $x$, the complex value $\exp(x+0i)$ equals the published real exponential $e^x$. The conventions and prerequisite facts used below are recorded in [[def-complex-exponential]], [[lem-complex-exponential-series-converges-everywhere]], [[lem-cauchy-product-of-absolutely-convergent-complex-series]], [[def-real-exponential-function-and-e]], [[lem-binomial-theorem-over-complex-numbers]], [[thm-binomial-closed-formula]].

**The factorial.** By the recursion theorem (The recursion theorem) applied to the
set $\mathbb{N}\times\mathbb{N}$, the starting element $(0,1)$ and the function
$f(k, v) = (\sigma(k),\, v \cdot \sigma(k))$, and by the same induction on the
first coordinate as in Finite sums and finite products of natural numbers, $\sum_{k<n} a_k$ and $\prod_{k<n} a_k$ in $\mathbb{N}$, there is a unique
$F : \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{N}$ with

$$F(0) = 1, \qquad F(\sigma(n)) = F(n)\cdot\sigma(n) \quad (n \in \mathbb{N}).$$

We write $n! := F(n)$. Thus $0! = 1$, $1! = 0!\cdot 1 = 1$, $2! = 1!\cdot 2 = 2$,
$3! = 6$, $4! = 24$, $5! = 120$, $6! = 720$.

**$0! = 1$ is the base clause of this recursion**, not a convention imported from
elsewhere. Nothing about empty products is presupposed; the agreement with the
empty product is proved below, in clause (a), rather than assumed.

**Truncated difference.** Throughout, $n - k$ is the operation fixed in
Finite sums and finite products of natural numbers, $\sum_{k<n} a_k$ and $\prod_{k<n} a_k$ in $\mathbb{N}$: the unique $j$ with $k + j = n$ when
$k \le n$, and $0$ when $n < k$.

**The falling factorial.** For $n \in \mathbb{N}$ define $n^{\underline{k}}$ by
recursion on $k$, by the recursion theorem applied to
$\mathbb{N}\times\mathbb{N}$ with starting element $(0,1)$ and
$f(k, v) = (\sigma(k),\, v \cdot (n-k))$:

$$n^{\underline{0}} = 1, \qquad n^{\underline{\sigma(k)}} = n^{\underline{k}}\cdot(n-k) .$$

So $n^{\underline{1}} = 1\cdot(n-0) = n$ and $n^{\underline{2}} = n\,(n-1)$, and
for $k \le n$ the value is the product $n(n-1)\cdots(n-k+1)$ of the $k$ topmost
factors.

**Four facts, proved here because the page uses each of them.**

**(a) The factorial is the product of the first $n$ positive naturals.**
$n! = \prod_{j<n}\sigma(j) = \prod_{j<n}(j+1)$, the $\mathbb{N}$-valued product of
Finite sums and finite products of natural numbers, $\sum_{k<n} a_k$ and $\prod_{k<n} a_k$ in $\mathbb{N}$. Induction (The principle of mathematical induction): at
$n = 0$ both sides are $1$, the empty product and the base clause agreeing; and
$\prod_{j<\sigma(n)}\sigma(j) = \big(\prod_{j<n}\sigma(j)\big)\cdot\sigma(n) = n!\cdot\sigma(n) = \sigma(n)!$.
**So the empty-product reading and the base-clause reading are the same reading**,
and neither was assumed.

**(b) $n! \ne 0$, and $\iota(n!) = \prod^{\mathbb{R}}_{j<n}\iota(j+1)$.** For the
first, $0! = 1 \ne 0$ (The von Neumann naturals form a Peano system) and
$\sigma(n)! = n!\cdot\sigma(n)$ is a product of two nonzero naturals, which is
nonzero: if $xy = 0$ with $y \ne 0$ then $xy = 0\cdot y$
(Zero and one under multiplication) and cancellation gives $x = 0$
(Cancellation for multiplication by a nonzero factor). So $n! \ne 0$ for every $n$ by induction. For the second, apply the bridge clause
6 of that lemma to clause (a) above. This is what makes the factorial of this
page and the real-valued product $\prod_{j<n}(j+1)$ used elsewhere in the library
**one object seen twice**, rather than two unrelated notions.

**(c) $n^{\underline{k}}\cdot(n-k)! = n!$ for $k \le n$.** Induction on $k$, for
all $n$ at once. At $k = 0$ this reads $1 \cdot n! = n!$. Assume it at $k$ and
let $\sigma(k) \le n$; then $k \le n$, and writing $d := n - k$ we have
$k + d = n$ and $d \ne 0$, since $k + 0 = k \ne n$; so $d = \sigma(e)$ for a
unique $e$ (Every nonzero natural number is a successor), and $\sigma(k) + e = n$, that is
$e = n - \sigma(k)$ (Addition is cancellative). Therefore
$n^{\underline{\sigma(k)}}\cdot\big(n-\sigma(k)\big)! = n^{\underline{k}}\cdot(n-k)\cdot e! = n^{\underline{k}}\cdot\big(e!\cdot\sigma(e)\big) = n^{\underline{k}}\cdot\sigma(e)! = n^{\underline{k}}\cdot(n-k)! = n!$,
using commutativity and associativity of multiplication
(Multiplication is associative, Multiplication is commutative) and the recursion
clause for the factorial.

**(d) Boundary values.** $n^{\underline{0}} = 1$ for every $n$, by the base
clause; $n^{\underline{n}} = n!$, since clause (c) at $k = n$ gives
$n^{\underline{n}}\cdot 0! = n!$ and $0! = 1$; and
$n^{\underline{k}} = 0$ whenever $k > n$. For the last, $n - n = 0$ gives
$n^{\underline{\sigma(n)}} = n^{\underline{n}}\cdot 0 = 0$, the clause
$x \cdot 0 = 0$ being definitional (Multiplication of natural numbers), and if
$n^{\underline{k}} = 0$ then
$n^{\underline{\sigma(k)}} = 0$ as well, so $n^{\underline{k}} = 0$ for every
$k \ge \sigma(n)$ by induction.

Let $a \in \mathbb{R}$, where $\mathbb{R}$ is the ambient ordered field
(Ordered field, Field).

**Natural exponents.** By the recursion theorem (The recursion theorem) applied to
the set $\mathbb{R}$, the starting element $1$ and the function
$f(x) = x \cdot a$, there is a unique function $\mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{R}$,
written $n \mapsto a^n$, with

$$a^0 = 1, \qquad a^{n+1} = a^n \cdot a \quad (n \in \mathbb{N}).$$

Thus $a^1 = a$, $a^2 = a \cdot a$, and so on. Note that this is defined for
**every** $a$, including $a = 0$.

**Negative exponents.** If $a \ne 0$ and $n \in \mathbb{N}$ with $n \ge 1$, set

$$a^{-n} := (a^n)^{-1}.$$

**Why that is legitimate.** The right-hand side presupposes that $a^n$ is
invertible, that is, that $a^n \ne 0$. This is a proof obligation and not an
observation, and it is discharged by claim 2 of Laws of integer exponents: for $a \ne 0$
in a field, $a^n \ne 0$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$, proved there by induction on
$n$ from the fact that a field has no zero divisors (A field has no zero divisors: $ab = 0 \Rightarrow a = 0$ or $b = 0$).
That lemma is a statement *about* the operation introduced here, so it depends on
this definition and is recorded in this item's `justified_by` rather than in its
`deps` (SCHEMA §3). Given $a^n \ne 0$, the value $(a^n)^{-1}$ is a single
well-determined element, because multiplicative inverses in a field are unique
(Identities and inverses in a field are unique).

**Integer exponents.** Every integer $m$ (The integers as equivalence classes of pairs of naturals) is either
$n$ or $-n$ for a unique natural $n$, where $n$ in these integer expressions denotes its image under the
embedding $\iota : \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{Z}$ (The naturals embed in the integers,
Arithmetic on the integers). This too is a citation and not a slogan: the order on
$\mathbb{Z}$ is total (The integers form a totally ordered ring), so $m \ge 0$ or $m < 0$; the
image of $\iota$ is exactly the set of nonnegative integers, and each of them is
$n$ for a unique natural $n$ (The naturals embed in the integers); and if $m < 0$ then
$-m > 0$, by compatibility of the order with addition (The integers form a totally ordered ring),
so $-m = n$ and $m = -n$, with $n$ unique because $\iota$ is
injective. The two clauses above therefore define $a^m$ for every
$m \in \mathbb{Z}$ whenever $a \ne 0$, and for every $m \in \mathbb{N}$ for
arbitrary $a$. The two exponent domains are disjoint: the natural clause
handles $m \ge 0$, including $m = 0$, while the negative clause requires
$n \ge 1$ and therefore handles only $m < 0$.

Use the transverse one-particle space $\mathcal H_T$ and multiplier $\omega(\mathbf k)$ of [[def-qft-qed-photon-energy-multiplier]], and form its symmetric Fock space $\mathcal F_s(\mathcal H_T)$. Let $H_{\rm ph}:=\hbar c\,d\Gamma(\omega)$, with $\hbar,c>0$ and $d\Gamma(\omega)$ acting on the $n$-particle sector as multiplication by $\sum_{j=1}^n|\mathbf k_j|$, as in [[lem-qft-second-quantized-spectrum]]. For a coherent vector use
$$ \epsilon(f):=\bigoplus_{n=0}^{\infty}\frac{f^{\otimes n}}{\sqrt{n!}},\qquad C(f):=e^{-\|f\|^2/2}\epsilon(f), $$
using the tensor and direct-sum conventions of [[def-qft-fock-and-test-spaces]].

Let $\kappa>0$. Let $b:S^2\to\mathbb C^3$ be measurable with $b\in L^2(S^2,d\Omega;\mathbb C^3)$, $\mathbf n\cdot b(\mathbf n)=0$ for a.e. $\mathbf n$, and
$$ C_b:=\int_{S^2}|b(\mathbf n)|^2\,d\Omega>0. $$
Take $\mathbf k,\kappa,\epsilon$ in inverse metres and $b$ dimensionless; then $f_\epsilon$ has momentum-wavefunction units $\mathrm m^{3/2}$, $C_b$ is dimensionless, and $\hbar c(\kappa-\epsilon)$ has energy units.
For $0<\epsilon<\kappa$, define $f_\epsilon(0)=0$ and
$$ f_\epsilon(\mathbf k):=\mathbf1_{\{\epsilon<|\mathbf k|<\kappa\}}|\mathbf k|^{-3/2}b\!\left(\frac{\mathbf k}{|\mathbf k|}\right). $$
Then
$$ \|f_\epsilon\|^2=C_b\log\frac{\kappa}{\epsilon},\qquad \langle C(f_\epsilon),H_{\rm ph}C(f_\epsilon)\rangle =\hbar c\,C_b(\kappa-\epsilon). $$
Each $C(f_\epsilon)$ is a unit vector in $D(H_{\rm ph})$. As $\epsilon\downarrow0$, $C(f_\epsilon)\rightharpoonup0$ weakly, but the family has no strong Fock-space limit. The statement is an exact free transverse-mode construction; it asserts no interacting charged sector, continuum QED limit, or empirical observation.

derivations.claim:
Put $\lambda=C\log(\Delta/\varepsilon)$. By [F2], the count
distribution is $p_m=e^{-\lambda}\lambda^m/m!$. Reindexing the nonnegative
series gives
$$\mathbb E N_{(\varepsilon,\Delta)} =e^{-\lambda}\sum_{m\ge1}\frac{m\lambda^m}{m!} =\lambda e^{-\lambda}\sum_{j\ge0}\frac{\lambda^j}{j!} =\lambda.$$
This calculation also gives zero mean when $C=0$ by [F9].

If $C>0$, fix $\Delta$ and set $\kappa=\Delta/c$ and $\delta=\varepsilon/c$. The Definition's profile $f_{\varepsilon,\Delta}$ is exactly the supplier profile with these cutoffs and the same transverse angular function $b$; its hypotheses hold because $\kappa>0$ and $C_b=C>0$. Applying [F10] shows that $\Psi_{\varepsilon,\Delta}$ has no strong Fock-space limit as $\varepsilon\downarrow0$.

If $C>0$, then for every integer $q\ge1$, whenever $\varepsilon<\Delta\,2^{-q}$, $\log(\Delta/\varepsilon)>q\log2\ge q/2$, since $\log2=\int_1^2dt/t\ge1/2$ by [F7]. Hence $C\log(\Delta/\varepsilon)\to\infty$ as $\varepsilon\downarrow0$. For $C=0$ the count and its mean remain zero.

Under the isometry in [F5], multiplication by $|\mathbf k|$ and by the
frequency-band indicator commutes pointwise with $P_T(\mathbf k)$,
so the scalar sector multiplier of [F5] restricts to the transverse Fock
space. On the support of $f_{\varepsilon,\Delta}$,
$0<\hbar c|\mathbf k|<\hbar\Delta$. By [F5], the squared norm of the
energy-operator image is bounded by
$$\|H_\gamma\Psi_{\varepsilon,\Delta}\|^2 \le(\hbar\Delta)^2e^{-\lambda} \sum_{m\ge0}\frac{m^2\lambda^m}{m!} =(\hbar\Delta)^2(\lambda^2+\lambda)<\infty.$$
The identity follows by writing $m^2=m(m-1)+m$ and shifting indices in
the two exponential series [F8], with [F9] covering $\lambda=0$.
Thus $\Psi_{\varepsilon,\Delta}\in D(H_\gamma)$.

On sector $m$, the energy multiplier is the sum of the $m$ one-particle
energies. Product tensor pairings make each summand contribute
$\langle f_{\varepsilon,\Delta},
\hbar c|\mathbf k| f_{\varepsilon,\Delta}\rangle
\|f_{\varepsilon,\Delta}\|^{2(m-1)}$. Including the coherent-state factor
and the sector normalization gives
$$\langle\Psi_{\varepsilon,\Delta},H_\gamma\Psi_{\varepsilon,\Delta}\rangle =e^{-\lambda}\sum_{m\ge1} \frac{m\langle f_{\varepsilon,\Delta}, \hbar c|\mathbf k| f_{\varepsilon,\Delta}\rangle\lambda^{m-1}}{m!} =\langle f_{\varepsilon,\Delta}, \hbar c|\mathbf k| f_{\varepsilon,\Delta}\rangle,$$
where $e^{-\lambda}\sum_{m\ge1}m\lambda^{m-1}/m!=1$ by [F8].
Polar coordinates [F6], $\nu=cr$, and the definition of $C$ give
$$\langle f_{\varepsilon,\Delta}, \hbar c|\mathbf k| f_{\varepsilon,\Delta}\rangle =\int_A|b(n)|^2d\Omega(n) \int_{\varepsilon/c}^{\Delta/c}\hbar c\,dr =\hbar C(\Delta-\varepsilon).$$
It is bounded by $\hbar C\Delta$ and tends to that finite value as
$\varepsilon\downarrow0$.

If $C=0$, [F1] gives $\|b\|_{L^2}^2=0$, so $b$ is the zero $L^2$ equivalence class and hence $b=0$ almost everywhere. The same radial norm calculation in [F2] gives $\|f_{\varepsilon,\Delta}\|^2=C\log(\Delta/\varepsilon)$. For $C>0$ this is unbounded as $\varepsilon\downarrow0$ by step 2.1. For $C=0$ the displacement is the zero $L^2$ vector at every cutoff by [F2].

In the defined finite-cutoff coherent model, let
$0<\varepsilon<\Delta<\Lambda$ and $C\ge0$. Let $N_u$ and $N_r$ be the
counts in the unresolved band
$(\varepsilon,\Delta)$ and resolved band $[\Delta,\Lambda)$,
respectively. The exclusive no-emission probability is
$$\mathbb P(N_u=0,N_r=0)= \exp\!\left(-C\log\frac{\Lambda}{\varepsilon}\right).$$
For every $n\in\mathbb N_0$,
$$\mathbb P(N_u=n,N_r=0)= \exp\!\left(-C\log\frac{\Lambda}{\varepsilon}\right) \frac{\left(C\log\frac{\Delta}{\varepsilon}\right)^n}{n!}.$$
Summing over all unresolved counts gives the finite-resolution inclusive
probability
$$\mathbb P(N_r=0)= \exp\!\left(-C\log\frac{\Lambda}{\Delta}\right),$$
which is independent of the lower cutoff $\varepsilon$. This is an exact
identity in the defined free coherent model; it does not assert real–virtual
cancellation in interacting QED or a detector's empirical response.

For $x>0$, $\log$ is differentiable and
$$\log'(x)=\frac1x,\qquad \log x=\int_1^x\frac{dt}{t}.$$
The exponential function is continuous and strictly increasing on $\mathbb R$.
